props.text: LEARNING GUIDE TO CLINICAL SKILLS I & II YEAR 1 MED112, MED115 (2022-2023) Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 1 of 64 Table of contents Topic Page number Hand Hygiene 4 Personal Protective Equipment 14 History taking 21 Vital signs 23 Measuring temperature 24 Measuring pulse rate 26 Measuring blood pressure 29 Heart sounds 33 Electrocardiogram (ECG) 37 Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) 43 Blood sample withdrawal 48 Intravenous injection 54 Insertion of urinary catheter 57 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 2 of 64 This course will help you achieve part of the following program competencies. The graduate as a health care provider •1.6 Take and record structured history from patient •1.7 Perform relevant systematic physical, neurological, and psychological examination The graduate as a professional •3.8Exhibit commitment to quality improvement and patient’s safety. The graduate as a lifelong learner and researcher •6.1 Develop, implement, monitor, and revise a personal learning plan to enhance professional practice•6.2 Explore opportunities and use various resources for learning.10% 10% 10% Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 3 of 64 By the end of this course, you will: • Become aware of rules and regulations in the clinical skills lab. • Reflect on the importance of hand hygiene. • Discuss WHO five moments of hand hygiene. • Perform effective alcohol hand rub in 30 seconds. • Don and doff personal protective equipment in the right way. • Reflect on the importance of taking a thorough history. • Discuss the different items of history; family history, medical history, drug history, and social history. • Take personal, present history, family history, medical history, drug history, and social history from a standardized patient. • Mention the different vital signs. • Measure patient’s body temperature. • Identify different locations for peripheral pulsation. • Measure and record radial pulse of the left arm of Simulated Model with precision ± four from actual measuring. • Measure and record radial pulse of a standardized patient with precision ± 4 from actual measuring. • Measure and record blood pressure both palpatory and auscultatory on right arm of Standardized patient using mercury sphygmomanometer with precision ± 5 mmHg from actual measuring. • Measure and record blood pressure both palpatory and auscultatory on simulated model using aneroid sphygmomanometer with precision ± 10 mmHg from actual measuring. • Perform 12 leads electrocardiogram application on Simulated model. • Interpret Lead II electrocardiogram reading. • Locate different heart auscultatory areas on simulation model. • Differentiate between normal and abnormal heart sounds. • Perform high quality compression only cardiopulmonary resuscitation on task trainer. • Perform venipuncture on simulation model taking into consideration infection control measures. • Perform Intravenous Injection on Simulation model taking into consideration drug safety measures and infection control measures. • Perform male and female urinary catheterization. • Apply all infection control measures to perform aseptic urinary catheter insertion. Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 4 of 64 HAND HYGIENE Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 5 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 6 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 7 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 8 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 9 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 10 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 11 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 12 of 64 Hand Hygiene (HH) Competency Learning Guide Routine hand wash Competency Learning Guide Procedure Competency Satisfactory Unsatisfactory Not performed 1. Wet hands with water 2. Apply enough soap to cover all hand surfaces 3. Rub hands palm to palm 4. Right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers and vice versa 5. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced 6. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked 7. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm and vice versa 8. Rotational rubbing, backwards and forwards with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm and vice versa 9. Rinse hands with water 10. Dry hands thoroughly with a single use towel, Use towel to turn off faucet Duration of procedure: 40-60 sec Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 13 of 64 Alcohol based hand rub Competency Learning Guide Procedure Competency Done Inadequate Not Done 1. Apply a palm-full of the product in a cupped hand, covering all surfaces 2. Rub hands palm to palm 3. Right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers and vice versa 4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced 5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked 6. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm and vice versa 7. Rotational rubbing, backwards and forwards with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm and vice versa 8. Leave to dry (repeat steps) Duration of procedure: 20-30 sec Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 14 of 64 PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 15 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 16 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 17 of 64 Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 18 of 64 Surgical masks donning and doffing competency Learning Guide Procedure Competency Donning Done Inadequate Not Done 1. Perform Hand hygiene 2. Find the top side of the mask (nose piece up) 3. Place over nose, mouth and chin to cover the face 4. Fit flexible nose piece over nose bridge 5. Secure on head with ties or elastic 6. Fit the mask to your face and under your chin 7. Adjust to fit without leaving gaps on the sides Doffing Done Inadequate Not Done 1. Perform Hand hygiene 2. Untie the bottom, then top, tie 3. Pull the face mask forward off the face to remove. 4. Discard in medical waste 5. Perform Hand hygiene Clinical Skills I & II (MED112, MED115) Page 19 of 64 Non-surgical disposable Gowns donning and doffing competency Learning Guide Procedure Competency Donning Done Inadequate Not Done 1. Perform Hand Hygiene 2. Hold the gown in front of you so the opening faces you. Slide your arms through the sleeves of the gown 3. Secure the gown: Tie all laces by a simple bow 4. Fully cover torso from neck to knees, arms to end of wrist, and rap around your back Doffing Done Inadequate Not Done 1. Perform Hand Hygiene 2. Unfasten all gown ties (take care that your sleeves do not reach your body when reaching the ties. 3. Touching inside the gown only, pull gown away from neck and shoulders 4. Turn gown inside out 5. Fold or roll the gown and discard in medical waste 6. Perform Hand Hygiene

props.text: 2 Table of Content pages Cranial nerves examination 6-14 Motor examination 15-18 Coordination and gait 18-22 Reflexes 23-29 Sensory examination 29-36 Vision 37-46 Suturing 47-62 Intramuscular Injection 63-66 Subcutaneous Injection 67-68 Intradermal Injection 69 Hearing 70-73 Airway management 74-79 Emergency care for choking 80-81 Nasogastric insertion 82-83 GIT symptomatology and local abdominal examination 84-105 Respiratory symptomatology and local respiratory examination 106-118 Cardiac symptomatology and local cardiac examination 109-130 Neurologic examination 3 Items to be fulfilled 1. PHYSICAL DEVELOPMENT& GENERAL APPEARANCE 2. MENTAL STATUS 3. SPEECH & ARTICULATION 4. CRANIAL NERVES 5. MOTOR EXAM 6. GAIT & COORDINATION 7. REFLEXES 8. SENSORY SYSTEM 9. TROPHIC & VASOMOTOR CHANGES 10. SKULL & SPINE EXAINATION 11. SPECIAL TESTS 12. GENERAL EXAMINATION A. General appearance and behavior  Physical development will indicate any gross endocrinal or nutritional disturbance. e.g. height, weight ▪ General appearance may be very helpful for early diagnosis, as the expressionless face of parkinsonism syndrome which may be evident before the appearance of the disease ▪ Age and concordance of appearance to age, Body build, Posture, Eye contact, Dress/grooming ▪ Alertness/attentiveness to the examiner: Physical features/abnormalities, Emotional facial expression ▪ General motor status: Retardation, Agitation, Abnormal movements, Gait  Pallor, jaundice etc. Neurologic examination 4 B. Mental state examination 1) State of consciousness Glasgow coma scale is the standard and should be assessed in every patient Glasgow Coma Scale 2) Intellectual functions I. Orientation (awareness to)  Person  Place  Time II. Attention & concentration  Ask the patient to Ability to count by serial 7‘s (subtract serial 7s from 100).  Ask the patient to name five things that start with a particular letter.  Ask the patient to rename days of week backward.  Ability to spell a word backward and forward III. Memory  Remote memory: ask about childhood data, important events known to have occurred when the patient was younger or free of illness.  Recent memory: the past few days what the patient had for breakfast, lunch, dinner.  Immediate retention or recall: digit span measures; ability to repeat six figures after examiner; ability to repeat three words 3 simple objects after 2 and 5 minutes (dog – cat – street) IV. Intelligence: mathematical problem- Educational and professional achievements (Average versus above average/below average) V. Insight: Awareness of the illness and its implications VI. Judgment: Ability to satisfactorily resolve a proposed hypothetical scenario utilizing good judgment VII. General knowledge Neurologic examination 5 3) Mood, Affect & Emotion Stability, Range, Appropriateness, Intensity, Mood (Experience and Expression) Behavior (expression): Aggressive, assertive, passive, and passive aggressive. Thought content: Suicidal ideation, Homicidal ideation, Depressive cognitions, Obsessions, Ruminations, Phobias, Ideas of reference, Paranoid ideation, Delusions C. Speech & articulation  Disturbance of speech is called, according to its severity, dysphasia or aphasia  Disturbance of articulation is called dysarthria, or anarthria  Speech examination: 1. Spontaneous speech a. Informal interview: Attention should be paid to the fluency of speech, presence of initiation difficulty, the presence of word-finding pauses. b. Structured task 2. Naming objects: tested by asking the patient to name objects, object parts, pictures, colors, or body parts to confrontation. 3. Repetition: Repetition of words and phrases should be deliberately tested. 4. Reading 5. Writing Simplified examination:  Receptive:  Auditory: Give the patient orders to do: start with one order then 2 orders, then 3 integrated complex orders  Visual: Give the patients the same orders written on the paper and tell him to do it.  Expressive Naming objects  Spoken.  Written. Types of aphasia or dysphasia:  Expressive aphasia (=motor=Broca‘s aphasia)  Receptive aphasia (=sensory =Wernicke‘s aphasia)  Global aphasia: no reception & no expression  Nominal aphasia: cannot name objects  Alexia: cannot read  Agraphia: cannot write.  Articulation examination: الفااححت alfatiha) Read  Repeating a long word with multiple syllables: أسكٌدريت  Count from 1-100 Neurologic examination 6 Dysarthria means only faulty articulation of speech sounds. It may result from central lesions of the brain or cerebellum, intoxications (such as alcohol), or neuromuscular disorders. Examiner should pay attention to different form of dysarthria for example slurred speech which occurs with lesions along the course of the pyramidal tr act, staccato or scanning speech which occurs in cerebellar lesion, low monotonous tone or nasal tone of voice etc. D. Cranial nerves examination The 12 pairs of cranial nerves (with the exception of the olfactory (I) pair and optic (II) pair arise from the brainstem). Cranial nerves II, III, IV and VI relate to the eye and the VIII nerve to hearing and balance. I. Olfactory nerve Function: Conveys the sense of smell. Examination: Ask the patient to close his eye. Test each nostril separately. Hold a non-irritant odor in front of the open nostril and ask him to sniff. Wait a moment for the patient to perceive the odor and then identify it. NB: Avoid the use of irritating substance as ammonia which will stimulate the trigeminal nerve. Abnormalities: Hyposmia (decreased sense of smell) or anosmia (inability to smell). Parosmia (the perception of pleasant odors as unpleasant).  The most frequent causes of anosmia are the common cold, COVID, allergic rhinitis, smoking, and head trauma.  Hyposmia also occurs in, Wernicke -Korsakoff syndrome, Kallman syndrome, Alzheimer‘s disease, Parkinson‘s disease and lesions of the olfactory bulbs and tracts like meningeal neoplasms- classically, olfactory groove meningiomas - that compress the olfactory bulbs and tracts. II. Optic nerve Function: vision The visual pathway consists of the retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tracts, lateral geniculate bodies, optic radiations and visual cortex. The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye. For pupillary constriction, the afferent pathway is the optic nerve. Examination: • VISUAL ACUITY: Counting Finger-Snellen Chart • VISUAL FIELDS: by the confrontation method Take a distance of 1 meter between the doctor &patients Then check the field from the periphery, from the 4 directions • FUNDOSCOPIC EXAM: Optic disc - Optic cup – Retinal vessels Neurologic examination 7 Abnormalities: Deficits in the visual pathway lead to specific field defects (Total loss of vision in one eye because of a lesion of the optic nerve). III Oculomotor, IV Trochlear, VI Abducent nerves Function: The upper lid is elevated by the levator palpebrae superioris, innervated by cranial nerve III. The six extraocular muscles are responsible for eye movements. Cranial nerve III innervates the superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles. Cranial nerve IV innervates the superior oblique muscle and cranial nerve VI innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Neurologic examination 8 Examination: 1. Palpebral fissures: detect any dropping of the upper eye lid (ptosis), or retraction of it. Also, observe the position of the eyes for any exophthalmos (proptosis) or enophthalmos. Detect any nystagmus in the position of rest. Looking to the examiner‘s hand which is held at the level of the palpebral fissure (straight ahead gaze), normally the upper eye lid covers 1/5th of the cornea. 2. Pupils: observe the size, equality of the two pupils, shape or regularity, and mobility or reaction both to light (direct and consensual) and to accommodation. 3. Ocular movements: these are tested both for horizontal and vertical movements, and for convergence. Observe any limitation of movement in any directio

props.name: Vital Signs: Pulse
props.text: Review Learning Guides for Measuring Radial Pulse before clinical skills session on Vital Signs Radial Pulse Vital signs are indicators of the basic functions of the body. Any physiological or pathological changes in the body functions would be reflected in the vital signs . The four main vital signs routinely checked by healthcare providers include: Body temperature Pulse rate Breathing rate (respiration) Blood pressure We will start by pulse rate What is the pulse rate? Pulse Rate: is measuring heartbeat by palpating a peripheral artery with the fingertip. The pulse rate is a measurement of the heart rate. This is the number of times the heart beats per minute. As the heart pushes blood through the arteries, the arteries expand and contract with the blood flow . Taking a pulse not only measures the heart rate but also can indicate the following: Heart rhythm Strength of the pulse The normal pulse rate for healthy adults ranges from 60- 100 beats per minute. Exercises, some illnesses and emotions could increase the heart rate. On the other hand, runners who do a lot of cardiovascular conditions may have a slower heart rate of 40 beats per minute. Pulse could be recorded from accessible arteries such as: Carotid Temporal Brachial Radial How to measure Radial pulse ? STEP CP PA NP Getting ready Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds. Wash hands Greet the patient, Stand on the right side, Introduce yourself to the patient, and Explain the procedure to the patient. Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm on his chest. The procedure Use the right hand to palpate the patient's left radial pulse and vice versa. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, about two centimeters proximal to the thenar eminence. Place the tips of the index, middle and ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel. Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: if regular, count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and if irregular, count for 3 minutes and divide by 3. After the procedure Wash the hands. Discuss the findings with the patient. Record the results as beats / minute and comment on regularity. Thank the patient. CP: Competently performed PA performed with Assistance NP ( not done)

In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. There is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Why do we use Stethoscope? Stethoscope Try to put your stethoscope on your radial or brachial artery would you hear anything? props.text: Vital Signs Radial Pulse Vital signs are indicators of the basic functions of body. A ny physiological or pathological changes in the body functions would be reflected on the vital signs The 4 main vital signs routinely checked by healthcare providers include: Body temperature Pulse rate Breathing rate (respiration) Blood pressure We will start by pulse rate What is pulse rate ? Pulse Rate: is measuring heartbeat by palpating a peripheral artery by the fingertip . The pulse rate is a measurement of the heart rate. This is the number of times the heart beats per minute. As the heart pushes blood through the arteries, the arteries expand and contract with the flow of the blood. Taking a pulse not only measures the heart rate, but also can indicate the following: Heart rhythm Strength of the pulse The normal pulse rate for health adults ranges from 60- 100 beats per minute. Exercises, some illness and emotions could increase the heart rate. On the other hand, runners who do a lot of cardiovascular conditions may have slower heart rate with 40 beats per minute. Pulse could be recorded from accessible arteries such as: C arotid T emporal B rachial R adial How to measure Radial pulse ? STEP CP P A NP Getting ready Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds. Wash hands Greet the patient, Stand on the right side, Introduce yourself to the patient, and Explain the procedure to the patient. Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm on his chest. The procedure Use the right hand to palpate the patient's left radial pulse and vice versa. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, about two centimeters proximal to the thenar eminence . Place the tips of the index, middle and ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel. Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: if regular, count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and if irregular, count for 3 minutes and divide by 3. After the procedure Wash the hands. Discuss the findings with the patient. Record the results as beats / minute and comment on regularity. Thank the patient. CP: Competently performed P A performed with A ssistance NP ( not done) II. Arterial Blood Pressure What is Blood Pressure Blood pressure is defined as the lateral pressure exerted by flowing blood on the walls of the arteries How is blood pressure measured? Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and is given as 2 figures: systolic pressure – the pressure when the heart pushes blood out diastolic pressure – the pressure when the heart rests between beats What are equipment needed for measuring blood pressure Sphygmomanometer There are different types of Sphygmomanometers Mercury Sphygmomanometer Mercury sphygmomanometers are made up of manually inflatable cuffs that are attached to measuring units with mercury-infused tubes. While operating the device, it is important to place the apparatus on a flat surface and in an upright position to get the correct readings. Aneroid Sphygmomanometer Aneroid means “without fluid,” and as the name suggests, this type of BP apparatus doesn’t make use of any mercury and is therefore considered the safest alternative to mercury sphygmomanometers. In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer The automatic digital sphygmomanometer is the most technologically-advanced sphygmomanometer design to date. These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. Similar to mercury and aneroid sphygmomanometers, digital sphygmomanometers also come with inflatable cuffs, but there is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Unlike the other two types, automatic digital sphygmomanometers evaluate and measure the fluctuations of arteries. Stethoscope III. Measuring Blood Pressure STEP/TASK CP AP NP Getting ready: Wash your hand Introduce yourself to the patient. Explain the procedure and obtain his consent. Tell him that he might feel some discomfort as the cuff is inflated, and that the blood pressure measurement may have to be repeated. Position The patient should be in the sitting position after 5 minutes rest. Three parts should be supported: back, feet and the arm. Ask the patient to expose the right arm by rolling up sleeve Attaching Blood Pressure Cuff Check that the blood pressure cuff size is appropriate for the patient's arm and that it is fully deflated Confirm the location of the brachial artery by palpating medial to the biceps brachii tendon and lateral to the medial epicondyle of the humerus Wrap the blood pressure cuff around the patient's upper arm, 2 cm above the antecubital fossa. Measuring blood pressure Position the BP measuring device so that it is roughly at the level of the patient’s heart. Position the measurement column/dial so that it is at eye level. Position the patient's right arm so that it is horizontal at the level of the midsternal and free from obstructive clothing. Measuring Blood Pressure Palpatory method Palpate the patient’s radial pulse, Inflate the blood pressure cuff until you can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. Note the reading on the sphygmomanometer at the point at which the radial pulse becomes impalpable. This reading is an approximate estimate of the patient's systolic blood pressure Open the valve and deflate the blood pressure cuff Close the valve on the blood pressure cuf f Measuring Blood Pressure Auscultatory Method Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery pulse, ensuring that it does not touch the cuff. Inflate the cuff to 20-30 mmHg more than the estimated systolic blood pressure (obliteration pressure). Then slowly deflate the cuff at around 2-3 mmHg per second The first consistent Korotkov sounds indicate the systolic blood pressure. The muffling and disappearance of the Korotkov sounds indicate the diastolic blood pressure. Record the blood pressure as the systolic reading over the diastolic reading. If the blood pressure is higher than 140/90, indicate that you might take a second reading after giving the patient a one minute rest. If the patient has a history of postural hypotension. you must also record the standing blood pressure To complete the procedure Once the blood pressure has been obtained, remove the blood pressure cuf f. Explain to the patient the procedure is complete Discuss the blood pressure results with the patient, including any further steps that may need to occur (e.g., follow-up, further investigations, initiation of treatment) Thank the patient Wash your hands Figure . props.name: PPT: EEG Revision
props.text: The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a measurement that enables us to detect the generalized activity of the cerebral cortex. Recorded from the surface of the scalp. The human EEG was first described by Austrian Psychiatrist Hans Berger in 1929. Electro Electrical encephalo Brain gram Picture Beta waves are observed in all age groups. They tend to be small in amplitude and usually are symmetric and more evident anteriorly. Beta is a ‘fast’ activity, present when we are alert, attentive , engaged in problem solving, judgment, decision making, and engaged in focused mental activity. Beta waves (12 to 30 Hz) Theta waves (3 to 8 Hz) Theta waves normally are seen in sleep at any age. In awake adults, these waves are abnormal if they occur in excess. Theta and delta waves are known collectively as slow waves. Theta brainwaves occur most often in sleep but are also dominant in deep meditation. Delta waves (3 Hz or less) They normally are seen in deep sleep , in adults as well as in infants and children. They have the largest amplitude of all waves. Delta brainwaves are slow, loud brainwaves. Brain produced all these waves all times, only the strength of the signal is dependent on the type of activity we are engaged in. K complex K complex waves are large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex. It signalling the onset of Stage N2 sleep Sleep spindles Like K-complexes, sleep spindles mark the onset of Stage N2 sleep and are usually seen against a generally slowed background. K complex Sleep spindle Questions Identify the wave. Normal frequency is------. Normally recoded in --------state. Recoded in which part of the brain . THANK YOU Collective synchronous activity of thousands of neurons are needed to create an EEG wave. They are signals generated when neurons send message to another. The quicker the firing, higher frequency of wave The more the neuron firing, more amplitude of the wave. EEG Rhythms Recording Brain Waves Recording an EEG is relatively simple, noninvasive, and it is painless. 24 or so electrodes taped to scalp at standard positions. they are fixed to standard positions on the head. and connected to banks of amplifiers and recording devices. EEG Setup Scalp Skull Dura mater Arachnoid mater Pia mater Cortex Subarachnoid space Pyramidal neuron Axon Dendrites - - - - + + + + Input from another area Electrode EEG Features of Normal Wakefulness- sleep in Adults Alpha waves generally are seen in all age groups but are most common in adults. They tend to be present posteriorly more than anteriorly and are especially prominent with closed eyes and with relaxation. Alpha activity disappears normally with attention ( eg , mental arithmetic, stress, opening eyes). Alpha is the resting state for the brain. Electromyography is a technique for evaluating and recording the electrical activity produced by skeletal muscles. It assess both muscle and nerve function. props.text: Brain Rhythm Abeer El- Emam Prof. of Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Alpha waves generally are seen in all age groups but are most common in adults. They tend to be present posteriorly more than anteriorly and are especially prominent with closed eyes and with relaxation. Alpha activity disappears normally with attention ( eg , mental arithmetic, stress, opening eyes). Alpha is the resting state for the brain. Alpha waves (8 to 12 Hz) Alpha wave (occipital) Beta waves are observed in all age groups. They tend to be small in amplitude and usually are symmetric and more evident anteriorly. Beta is a ‘fast’ activity, present when we are alert, attentive , engaged in problem solving, judgment, decision making, and engaged in focused mental activity. Beta waves (12 to 30 Hz) Theta waves (3 to 8 Hz) Theta waves normally are seen in sleep at any age. In awake adults, these waves are abnormal if they occur in excess. Theta and delta waves are known collectively as slow waves. Theta brainwaves occur most often in sleep but are also dominant in deep meditation. Delta waves (3 Hz or less) They normally are seen in deep sleep , in adults as well as in infants and children. They have the largest amplitude of all waves. Delta brainwaves are slow, loud brainwaves. Brain produced all these waves all times, only the strength of the signal is dependent on the type of activity we are engaged in. Slow Wave (or non-REM) Sleep Stage 1,2,3 REM-Sleep. STAGES OF SLEEP 17-Nov-25 15 17-Nov-25 16 K complex K complex waves are large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex. It signalling the onset of Stage N2 sleep Sleep spindles Like K-complexes, sleep spindles mark the onset of Stage N2 sleep and are usually seen against a generally slowed background. K complex Sleep spindle EXPERIMENTAL OBJECTIVES To record EEG from an awake, resting subject with their eyes open and eyes closed To observe interruptions of alpha rhythm during performance of mental math To observe temporary interruptions of alpha rhythm, following opening of the eye To identify and examine the alpha, beta, delta, and theta components of the EEG complex. Recording Brain Waves Recording an EEG is relatively simple, noninvasive, and it is painless. 24 or so electrodes taped to scalp at standard positions. they are fixed to standard positions on the head. and connected to banks of amplifiers and recording devices. Recording Brain Waves Measurements of individual neurons is not possible from the scalp, but the activity of collections of neurons is possible. Categorization of rhythms based on frequency. Sites of Electrode Placement MATERIALS BIOPAC electrode lead set (SS2L) BIOPAC Disposable Electrodes (EL503,) 3 electrodes per subject BIOPAC Electrode Gel (GEL1) and Abrasive Pad (ELPAD) or Skin cleanser or alcohol prep Biopac Student Lab System: BSL 4 software, MP36, MP35 or MP45 hardware Computer system (Windows or Mac) Hints for obtaining optimal data  As much as possible, move the hair away from the electrode area to ensure the electrode makes contact with the scalp.  Apply some gel to the electrode.  Apply pressure to the electrodes for about 1 minute after the initial placement.  Subject must remain still. Blinking and other movement will affect the recording of all four rhythms. Recording 1- Relaxed with eyes closed Recording 2- Performing mental math with eyes closed Recording 3- Relaxed with eyes open Recording 4- Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. Recording steps Instruct the Subject to relax with eyes closed, not thinking about anything (not fixing attention on any mental object). Click "Start" to begin recording. Continue recording and observe the corresponding plot, primarily expressing alpha rhythm, for one or two minutes. Press the F9 key to insert a marker while telling the Subject to open his eyes. Wait a few seconds and then insert another marker while telling the Subject to close his eyes. Tell the Subject to close his eyes and relax. Inform the Subject that he will be asked to perform mental math. Example: Count backward from 30 by subtracting increasing odd numbers (e.g., 30, 29, 26, 21). Running the Experiments Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. recording is resumed as quickly as possible after Subject has hyperventilated. However, to avoid EMG artifact, make sure Subject has stopped hyperventilating prior to clicking Record. As soon as Subject stops hyperventilating and is sitting still, Click Record immediately. Record for 10 seconds. Click Suspend. Hyperventilation evoke generalized slowing of EEG and elicit any abnormality When a person hyperventilates (breathes rapidly and deeply), too much carbon dioxide is eliminated from the blood, causing the blood and the cerebrospinal fluid that bathes the brain to become too alkaline. These changes increase the overall electrical activity of the brain including the amplitude of alpha waves Recording after hyperventilation The brain is continually active, even in the absence of environmental and body derived stimuli. Recorded from the surface of the scalp. The human EEG was first described by Austrian Psychiatrist Hans Berger in 1929. Electro Electrical encephalo Brain gram Picture Collective synchronous activity of thousands of neurons are needed to create an EEG wave. They are signals generated when neurons send message to another. The quicker the firing, higher frequency of wave The more the neuron firing, more amplitude of the wave. EEG Rhythms The extracellular voltage change within the cortex which recorded by scalp electrodes is largely derived from the excitatory and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs ), not from the neuronal action potentials. This is because, although action potentials are of much greater voltage, they are very brief , whereas the EPSPs and IPSPs are of much longer duration and hence, can summate to create a signal capable of being detected on the surface of the scalp through the resistance of the overlying tissues. props.text: Measuring and Recording Blood Pressure What is blood pressure? Blood pressure is defined as the lateral pressure exerted by flowing blood on the walls of the arteries 101 Physiology of blood pressure Blood inside artery will put a pressure on the wall Blood flow inside arteries Heart contracts push blood in arteries 101 Physiology of blood pressure Blood will put a maximum pressure which is systole Maximum blood will go into arteries Heart contracts 101 Physiology of blood pressure Blood will put a a least pressure which is diastole blood will go from arteries to veins Heart relaxes Blood Pressure Systolic Diastolic = 120 80 Maximum pressure inside the artery when heart contracts Least pressure inside the artery when heart relax How we measure Blood Pressure Equipements Stethoscope Sphygmomanometer Mercury Sphygmomanometer Are made up of manually inflatable cuffs that are attached to measuring units with mercury-infused tubes. While operating the device, it is important to place the apparatus on a flat surface and in an upright position to get the correct readings. Aneroid Sphygmomanometer Aneroid means “without fluid,” and as the name suggests, this type of BP apparatus doesn’t make use of any mercury and is therefore considered the safest alternative to mercury sphygmomanometers. In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. There is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Why do we use Stethoscope? Stethoscope Try to put your stethoscope on your radial or brachial artery would you hear anything? Korotkoff sounds What we would here Systolic Diastolic = 120 80 Maximum pressure First sound to hear after releasing pressure of cuff Least pressure Last sound to hear while deflating cuff https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM So let us measure the blood pressure https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6HtqolhKqo&t=44s Before the procedure Wash hands Introduce yourself Explain procedure Explain to the patients they might feel discomfort from the cuff but not painful Patient position Setting down on chair if they can after 5 minutes rest Back , leg and arm supported Ask the patients to expose the right arm by rolling up their sleeves Attaching cuff Should be right size Deflated 2cm above antecubital fossa Measuring blood pressure First method is: Palpatory method to get estimated (rough value ) systolic blood pressure Palpate the patient’s radial pulse Inflate the blood pressure cuff until you can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. Note the reading on the sphygmomanometer at the point at which the radial pulse becomes impalpable ( this point is estimated systolic blood pressure) Deflate the cuff till zero Close the valve Measuring blood pressure Second method is: Auscultatory method to get actual systolic and diastolic reading Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery pulse, ensuring that it does not touch the cuff. Inflate the cuff to 20-30 mmHg more than the estimated systolic blood pressure (obliteration pressure). Then slowly deflate the cuff at around 2-3 mmHg per second The first consistent Korotkov sounds indicate the systolic blood pressure. The muffling and disappearance of the Korotkov sounds indicate the diastolic blood pressure. Record the blood pressure as the systolic reading over the diastolic reading. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM To complete procedure Completely deflate the cuff Remove the cuff and blood pressure device Tell the patient readings and explain the significance Record reading in patient file Thank patient Wash your hand https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6HtqolhKqo&t=44s

Delta waves (3 Hz or less) They normally are seen in deep sleep, in adults as well as in infants and children. They have the largest amplitude of all waves. Delta brainwaves are slow, loud brainwaves. Brain produced all these waves all times, only the strength of the signal is dependent on the type of activity we are engaged in. K complex K complex waves are large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex. It signalling the onset of Stage N2 sleep Sleep spindles Like K-complexes, sleep spindles mark the onset of Stage N2 sleep and are usually seen against a generally slowed background. K complex Sleep spindle Recording Brain Waves Recording an EEG is relatively simple, noninvasive, and it is painless. 24 or so electrodes taped to scalp at standard positions. they are fixed to standard positions on the head. and connected to banks of amplifiers and recording devices. Recording Brain Waves Measurements of individual neurons is not possible from the scalp, but the activity of collections of neurons is possible. Categorization of rhythms based on frequency. Normal EEG EEG Rhythms During Sleep Seizures are caused by massive synchronous activity that spreads. Epilepsy is repeated occurrences of seizures. General seizure – entire cortex involved as synchronous firing spreads all over Partial seizure – localized in a brain area Seizures Generalized Epileptic Seizure MATERIALS BIOPAC electrode lead set (SS2L) BIOPAC Disposable Electrodes (EL503,) 3 electrodes per subject BIOPAC Electrode Gel (GEL1) and Abrasive Pad (ELPAD) or Skin cleanser or alcohol prep Biopac Student Lab System: BSL 4 software, MP36, MP35 or MP45 hardware Computer system (Windows or Mac) HINTS FOR OBTAINING OPTIMAL DATA ♣ As much as possible, move the hair away from the electrode area to ensure the electrode makes contact with the scalp. ♣ Apply some gel to the electrode. ♣ Apply pressure to the electrodes for about 1 minute after the initial placement. ♣ Subject must remain still. Blinking and other movement will affect the recording of all four rhythms. Recording 1- Relaxed with eyes closed Recording 2- Performing mental math with eyes closed Recording 3- Relaxed with eyes open Recording 4- Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. Recording steps Instruct the Subject to relax with eyes closed, not thinking about anything (not fixing attention on any mental object). Click "Start" to begin recording. Continue recording and observe the corresponding plot, primarily expressing alpha rhythm, for one or two minutes. Press the F9 key to insert a marker while telling the Subject to open his eyes. Wait a few seconds and then insert another marker while telling the Subject to close his eyes. Tell the Subject to close his eyes and relax. Inform the Subject that he will be asked to perform mental math. Example: Count backward from 30 by subtracting increasing odd numbers (e.g., 30, 29, 26, 21). Running the Experiments Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. recording is resumed as quickly as possible after Subject has hyperventilated. However, to avoid EMG artifact, make sure Subject has stopped hyperventilating prior to clicking Record. As soon as Subject stops hyperventilating and is sitting still, Click Record immediately. Record for 10 seconds. Click Suspend. Hyperventilation evoke generalized slowing of EEG and elicit any abnormality When a person hyperventilates (breathes rapidly and deeply), too much carbon dioxide is eliminated from the blood, causing the blood and the cerebrospinal fluid that bathes the brain to become too alkaline. These changes increase the overall electrical activity of the brain including the amplitude of alpha waves Recording after hyperventilation Recording after hyperventilation Recording during mental math Alpha block THANK YOU
